assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Assume a coloring f satisfies the circumcenter-closure hypothesis. Fix any point O and let c=f(O). Suppose some point G has the opposite color. Around the pair O,G, use L4 to build five auxiliary points X_i on the circle centered at G through O, each supported by a distinct pair A_i,B_i of points on the circle centered at O through G. By L2, the circle centered at O can contain at most two points of the color opposite to c; since the ten supporting points A_i,B_i are distinct, at least three support pairs are entirely colored c. For each such pair, L5 transfers color c from O to the corresponding X_i. Thus the circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying L1 to those three points forces G itself to have color c, contradicting that G had the opposite color. Hence no opposite-colored point exists; all points have color c. This is exactly the root theorem.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the monochromatic-circumcenter hypothesis. Choose an arbitrary point O and call its color c. To prove the coloring is constant, assume there exists a point G of the other color. Let r=dist(O,G)>0 and choose the small radius s=r/4, so 0<s<r/2. By the finite geometric configuration lemma, we can select five distinct auxiliary points X_1,...,X_5 on the small circle centered at G of radius s, and for each X_i two support points A_i,B_i on the large circle centered at O of radius r, with all ten support points pairwise distinct and arranged so that X_i is the circumcenter of triangle O A_i B_i. Because the large circle is centered at O, the circle bound lemma implies that at most two of these ten support points can have the color opposite to c. A simple pigeonhole argument then gives at least three indices i for which both A_i and B_i have color c. For each such index, the color-transfer lemma shows that X_i must also have color c, because X_i is the circumcenter of the monochromatic triangle O A_i B_i. Thus the small circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying the circle-center lemma to that circle forces G itself to have color c, contradicting the choice of G as opposite-colored. Therefore no opposite-colored point exists, so every point of the plane has color c. Since f was arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

steps.derives: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 fixed an arbitrary coloring f under the theorem hypothesis, and A12 established exactly the desired conclusion for that arbitrary f.

shared_context.content: For noncollinear points A,B,C in the Euclidean plane R^2, circumcenter(A,B,C) denotes the unique point equidistant from A,B,C.
shared_context.label: Circumcenter notation

shared_context.content: For a point Z in R^2 and a real number r>0, Circle(Z,r) means the set {P in R^2 | dist(P,Z)=r}, where dist is Euclidean distance.
shared_context.label: Circle notation

shared_context.content: A coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfies the monochromatic-circumcenter property if for every noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, whenever f(A)=f(B)=f(C), one has f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A).
shared_context.label: Root hypothesis schema

full_candidate.strategy_summary: Use a local contradiction from two opposite-colored points together with a finite auxiliary-circle configuration. This explicitly fixes the earlier fatal errors by avoiding any false global classification of circumcenter-closed subsets, and it also repairs the previous interface gap by using the exact support-point geometry needed for color transfer from a fixed point O to auxiliary points X_i on a small circle around G.

missing_coverage: The decomposition is missing a usable color-transfer lemma matching the L4 geometry. What A9 needs is a lemma of the form: if O!=X, A!=B, dist(O,A)=dist(O,B), and dist(X,A)=dist(X,B)=dist(O,X), then X is the circumcenter of triangle OAB, so f(O)=f(A)=f(B) implies f(X)=f(O). Current L3 is too strong and does not cover the configuration produced by A6.

previous_attempt_summaries.vet_summary: L1, L2, L4, and L5 are plausibly true, and L3 is likely true as stated, but the assembly fails at the key color-transfer step. Step A9 tries to apply L3 using the configuration from A6, yet A6 does not provide the metric equalities required by L3. The proof therefore never justifies that any X_i has color c, so the contradiction at G is not obtained.
